item.title: AI Can Simulate Empathy, but It Can’t Replace Psychotherapy
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Can Simulate Empathy, but It Can’t Replace Psychotherapy

Psychological change requires something AI cannot give: a genuine relationship.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • AI chatbots can simulate empathy and validation, making it easier to disclose feelings we struggle to express.
  • Genuine psychotherapy involves discomfort, conflict, and emotional work that AI cannot replicate.
  • Lasting change requires being known over time, not simply receiving support, advice, or affirmation.

A few months ago, NPR ran the story, “She told no one about her agony except ChatGPT. What her death reveals about AI risks.”1 What’s heartbreaking about the article is that the woman who died by suicide, Sophie Rottenberg, had a human psychotherapist, and yet her use of the AI therapist was so engrossing that she didn’t share her suicidal feelings with her living, human psychotherapist.

Sadly, Rottenberg is not an anomaly and instead points to something occurring far too regularly. In my last blog, I introduced the concept of the cultural unconscious to describe an underlying dimension of psychological life shaped by our shared cultural experiences. It encompasses collective images, practices, beliefs, and conflicts that circulate within a culture without complete conscious awareness.

The cultural unconscious shapes how we perceive ourselves and others, interpret our experiences, and engage with the world. One dominant cultural experience expressed in the cultural unconscious is what Dr. Sherry Turkle, MIT professor of the social studies of science and technology and a clinical psychologist, calls a “flight from conversation.” She argues in her book Reclaiming Conversation: The Power of Talk in a Digital Age that our constant tether to smartphones and digital devices has triggered it.2

We communicate more through texts, emails, and social media, but we connect less. We aren’t having as many spontaneous, face-to-face, and depthful conversations in real time. Instead, we’re inundated with numerous, remote, superficial messages that interrupt our attention—texts, tweets, alerts, snaps, emails—which are disconnected from organic, human dialogue.2 It is nearly inescapable in our culture. Turkle cites research showing that the mere presence of a phone—even a silent phone on a table—alters the quality of a conversation, keeps topics more superficial, and lowers empathy.

Why People Turn to AI for Emotional Support

As chatbots become more embedded in our culture, people are naturally turning to them for connection and mental health support. Conversation requires work, sustained attention, and engagement. It can be hard to be vulnerable with someone in real time, which often brings fear of judgment. Chatbots are a ready-made solution: instantly available, inexpensive, highly responsive, and offering responses that frequently align with what we hope to hear.

With the ease and accessibility of ChatGPT and Claude, more people are confessing what they may be too scared, ashamed, or psychologically defended to say out loud to another human being, even a psychotherapist. This fear and shame are magnified by critical public discourse that pushes this behavior underground, which can become even more dangerous when concealed. Secretive AI chatting feeds tragic situations we keep reading about—people committing suicide, not taking their medications, believing delusions, and more.

Again, part of AI’s allure is that it’s nonjudgmental and affirming, proclaiming, “Great idea,” and “You’re so right.” Such responses can be seductive both to people who feel inferior and/or superior. AI can bolster those who feel inferior while affirming those who feel superior, a dynamic that resonates with a 2026 study linking higher narcissism, individualism, and intolerance of uncertainty to more problematic AI use.3 For someone struggling with self-worth (i.e., narcissism), the assurance of being met with acceptance and praise can be intoxicating. So, too, is the illusion of empathy that AI provides. Genuine empathy is not synonymous with agreement or approval. Yet the human mind can conflate feeling understood with being validated, mistaking empathic understanding for affirmation of beliefs and behaviors.

If a person is struggling, they often want empathy reflected back, and many humans cannot consistently communicate that way. AI has been trained to produce the language of empathy, which many people lack in their relationships. However, AI cannot offer the relational and psychological processes that make empathy transformative, as it does in psychotherapy.

Initially, when AI responds with “That sounds so hard,” it may sound like music to one’s ears, especially when someone gets dismissive comments like “Sorry to hear that” from others in their life. When someone longs for care and understanding, a machine that says exactly what we want to hear can be comforting for a time. However, these affirming responses can only go so far, particularly when someone is suffering psychologically.

The psychological tools, education, and support that AI provides should not be confused with genuine psychotherapy. Despite having no professional qualifications, Rottenberg’s chatbot was touted as a highly knowledgeable therapist and introduced itself as “I am Harry, your personal therapist, and I’m here to support you.” As an AI chatbot, Harry simulated the language, empathy, and authority of a psychotherapist, but lacked the clinical judgment, relational responsibility, and ethical accountability required of licensed psychotherapists. Harry encouraged Rottenberg to seek help, create a safety plan, and confide in loved ones, but as a chatbot, it could not call her parents, alert authorities, or escalate the situation. Nor could it offer the relational, nuanced experience that human connection provides.

What Psychotherapy Offers Beyond Emotional Support

A common misconception is that psychotherapy primarily provides emotional support, a place to vent, problem-solving, advice, tools, or answers. Some people only experience this, reinforcing the belief that this is what psychotherapy primarily offers. In part, this is happening more frequently as therapy sessions are limited, psychotherapist training programs fail to educate comprehensively, and clinicians are overworked and undercompensated. As I’ve written about the limits of diagnosis, “being in treatment” involves knowing and being known. It’s being followed longitudinally and is not merely a place to vent or receive advice. Lasting psychological change requires more than these interventions.

Research highlights the importance of the therapeutic relationship and distinct therapeutic processes that support longer-term, meaningful change, including engaging with emotional experience, fostering insight, strengthening relational capacities, and helping individuals recognize and transform entrenched patterns.

Unlike chatting with AI, a skilled, ethical, and effective psychotherapist won’t offer complete understanding, affirmation, and unequivocal support. Rather, real psychotherapy includes relational conflict, pushback, discomfort, and difficult or negative emotions. Working through these challenges is central to psychotherapy. It’s a fluid, dynamic, and emergent process that unfolds between psychotherapist and patient, with each bringing their own reactions, emotions, and thoughts into the therapeutic container.

Chatting with AI comes with real issues and risks, yet AI can offer psychological education and support. It’s important to remember it cannot provide psychotherapy, although it can be a helpful adjunct. In my next post, I’ll explore issues related to AI and psychotherapy, including a case study in which AI enhanced the therapeutic process.

item.title: The Most Dangerous Compliment You Can Receive
item.description:
Relationships

The Most Dangerous Compliment You Can Receive

The perils of praise with a price.

Posted November 20, 2026

Key points
  • Flattery that does not match reality is inherently suspect.
  • Recipients may reward praise, inadvertently compromising perception.
  • Praise with a price often pairs professed admiration with an "ask."
  • Manipulators may pair adulation with criticism-keeping the recipient insecure.

We have probably all met someone along the way who impressed and attracted us with their charm, charisma, and positive attention. Yet at times, they may have made us feel unsettled with their praise. Their flattery may have been enjoyable at the beginning, but over time, some of the compliments may have gone over the top and made us uncomfortable. From our “stunning” appearance to our “brilliant” intellect, the acclaim was unmerited and even arguably untrue. What is their motivation? Research investigates this question.

Source: Image by erwin bosman from Pixabay

The Seduction of Selective Attention: Motives Matter

In the course of my almost 30 years as a prosecutor, I have observed one of the most seductive techniques used by sexual predators and human traffickers to be targeting young women who are not used to receiving positive attention. Having grown up in the shadow of much prettier peers and classmates, they are uniquely vulnerable to the unmerited compliments and advances of handsome (usually much older) men. Yet this dynamic is not limited to criminal perpetrators; it is used in everyday life by people seeking to manipulate and exploit people and resources.

Recognizing Praise With a Price

Benjamin A. Rogers et al. (2023) discussed the impact of praise in a study entitled, “Too Naïve to Lead: When Leaders Fall for Flattery.”[1] They identify flattery as one of the “oldest and most commonly used” tactics of impression management, one that frequently benefits the flatterer. Yet flattery also impacts the recipient, who may reward the praise, inadvertently compromising their perception. Managers are apparently not immune from this dynamic, as Rogers et al. note that when they reward flatterers, they risk being viewed as naïve. And “falling for flattery” can compromise impressions of both leaders and the organizations they represent.

Yet if you know what to look for, you can detect it.

How to Detect False Flattery

As a practical matter, false compliments often target idealized traits you would love to have but know you do not. A false flatterer will comment on your gorgeous figure or uncanny knack for solving complex problems—with very little or no evidence to support their compliments. In such instances, motivation is inherently suspect. “What do you want?” you might ask jokingly, when, actually, that is a very good question. Because many compliments are paired with an “ask,” requesting us to do something for the praise-giver, which puts their motivation under greater scrutiny. This is especially suspect when your denial of the request is met with hostility or expressions of disappointment.

The more challenging example is when you receive compliments in borderline areas where you may indeed possess some degree of the appearance or aptitude alleged. Here, we wonder whether our vocal admirer is merely viewing us with positive bias through rose-colored glasses. Yet if that is the case, they are unlikely to include a request, and certainly not become hostile or rude when we refuse.

Another red flag is mixing praise with criticism. This method of manipulation is designed to make us unsteady and anxious, leading some people to feel the need to behave in a certain way in order to be rewarded with flattery, instead of disheartened by criticism.

So, whether you are the boss or a new employee, a friend or potential paramour, keep your emotional antenna up both professionally and personally, and receive praise responsibly.

item.title: Did Darwin Kill the Meaning of Life?
item.description:
Philosophy

Did Darwin Kill the Meaning of Life?

Evolution leaves no room for cosmic purpose. Nietzsche saw it first.

Posted November 20, 2026

When asked in school what the meaning of life could possibly be, my friends and I answered "reproduction," seeing this as the natural conclusion of the truth of evolution. As faulty as this view of me and my friends was, it was based on the view that the evolutionary "purpose" of life is essentially reproduction. This, however, is usually not what is asked when faced with the question of what the meaning of life is, or rather what makes life meaningful. What is asked for, though, is some kind of higher, eternal purpose for humans. This is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic.

Existential Nihilism

The strongest argument for existential nihilism has been provided by the naturalist philosopher Daniel Dennett in Darwin’s Dangerous Idea: Evolution and the Meanings of Life. Evolution as a random and blind mechanism involving nothing beyond reproduction, variation, and differential reproductive success is the fundamental law of biology. Natural selection explains the origin of life and man, without any reference to purpose.

However, and from here existentialists get their name, evolution denies these kinds of essences that have "plagued" philosophy since Plato. Everything is in constant change under the blind and random mechanism of evolution. There is no essence, such as rationality or moral sense, that we could attribute to human nature. When Sartre famously remarked that “existence precedes essence,” he meant that it is left for humans themselves to decide who they are.

To sum up: Evolution destroys all notions of teleology in the biological realm. Sommers and Rosenberg, in their review paper of Dennett with the fitting title “Darwin’s nihilistic idea: evolution and the meaninglessness of life,” phrase the conclusions of the Darwinian argument for existential nihilism in the following way:

Darwinism thus puts the capstone on a process which since Newton’s time has driven teleology to the explanatory side-lines. In short, it has made Darwinians into metaphysical Nihilists denying that there is any meaning or purpose to the universe, its contents and its cosmic history.

The theory of evolution dissolves all purposes in, as Dennett puts it, “Darwin's universal acid”: science, therefore, renders God oblivious and takes away the illusion of purpose from our lives. Dennett even goes so far as to attribute the origin of existentialism to Darwin:

Friedrich Nietzsche saw—through the mists of his contempt for all things English—an even more cosmic message in Darwin: God is dead. If Nietzsche is the father of existentialism, then perhaps Darwin deserves the title of grandfather.

Nietzsche’s Darwinism

When Nietzsche proclaimed that “God is dead,” we are supposed to view science, if not as the murderer then at least as the tool that was used to kill God. While Nietzsche is often taken as a deterrent to where Darwinian philosophy leads, I argue that Nietzsche’s Darwinism is better associated with his ideas about the death of God than with the Übermensch. Even though Nietzsche is often given as an example of a nihilist, most of his work is directed against the destructive consequences of nihilism, once God has been replaced by science, or more accurately, where science left a hole after getting rid of God.

article continues after advertisement

Especially after the horrors of WW2, it is only reasonable to ask how anyone could continue to believe that there is a God or purpose to our lives. Much of existential thinking boils down to the fact, that there is no God and hence, no one to give the universe purpose and meaning to our lives.

Thomas Nagel offers a thought experiment in which humanity realizes that the human race and our whole planet were created by some creatures to farm and eat human flesh. Clearly, he argues, this doesn’t give us the purpose we ask for when asking for the meaning of life. Would the analogy change if it was God who created us for some purpose rather than a powerful alien race? Camus suggests that this may not work either: “I know that I do not know that meaning and that it is impossible for me just now to know it. What can a meaning outside my condition mean to me? I can understand only in human terms.” Even if God exists and has some purpose for us in mind, we cannot grasp it.
